analysis.one_liner: Requires banks and credit unions to get written customer consent before sharing personal financial information.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House Banking subcommittee with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed federal banking regulators to write rules requiring banks, savings associations, credit unions, and their parent companies to protect customers' financial information. It would have required them to tell customers when personal financial data was being collected or handed to another company, and to get a customer's written consent before sharing it — except when needed to provide the customer's own service or required by law.
analysis.who_benefits: Customers of banks, savings associations, and credit unions. Anyone with a bank account would gain control over who sees their financial records: the bill required notice whenever information was collected or offered to others, and affirmative written consent before it could be shared with affiliates, agents, or outside companies [S3]. Today that kind of sharing feeds marketing, telemarketing, and profiling based on account activity.

how_it_helps.text: Banks, savings associations, credit unions, and holding-company affiliates would be required to protect the confidentiality of customer financial information under regulations written by federal banking agencies [S2] [S3].
Institutions would have to inform customers whenever financial information about them was being collected or was going to be offered to any other person, including an affiliate or agent [S3].

Sharing or use of individually identifiable financial data would be allowed only for providing the service it came from, with the customer's affirmative written consent, or when required by law or a regulator — an opt-in standard, not merely an option to opt out [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, savings associations, credit unions, and bank and savings-and-loan holding companies. They would bear the cost of compliance programs and would lose the ability to freely use, sell, or share customer account data for marketing or other purposes, including across affiliates within a conglomerate [S3].

drawbacks.text: Compliance would impose real costs on regulated institutions, and community banks and small credit unions — which have fewer staff to build consent-tracking and data-protection systems — would feel them most; those costs can be passed to customers through fees.

An opt-in standard is stricter than the notice-and-chance-to-object approach many in the industry preferred; banks argued it could disrupt cross-selling of bundled products and services that some customers find convenient, and could raise the cost of offering them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — customers deciding who sees their financial records, with written consent required before sharing — is broad and touches nearly every household. The costs are compliance burdens concentrated on financial institutions, heaviest for small ones, and some limits on data-driven marketing and bundled products. The bill was a straightforward privacy protection, though like any mandate its practical strength depended on the regulations regulators would write.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Banking Committee, which passed it along to a subcommittee, and nothing further happened before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey introduced the bill on March 25, 1999 [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services the same day, and on April 16, 1999 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors [S4], and no further action appears in the record before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and other financial institutions, which kept the freedom to use and share customer account data without customers' written consent.

for.name: Rep. Edward J. Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Banking and Financial Services
against.role: Standing committee with jurisdiction over banking bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors on either side, so the partisan shape of support and opposition never appears in the record [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have forced them to build consent and notice systems and stopped them from freely sharing or selling customer account data for marketing. Their interest in keeping that freedom ran directly against customers' control over their own information.

industries.industry: Bank holding companies and savings-and-loan holding companies, including affiliates
industries.note: Conglomerates were expanding into combined banking, securities, and insurance, and sharing customer data across affiliates was a central benefit of that structure; the bill would have restricted that sharing unless the customer consented in writing.
Credit unions would have faced the same confidentiality, notice, and written-consent requirements for member data, a compliance cost falling hardest on smaller institutions.
